media.title: Will It Always Happen?
media.context: This is the chapter opener and it plays before any objective. It covers the textbook's opening on patterns that hold and shortcuts nobody can explain, and withholds every method: no place value argument, no divisibility test and no proof. Students arrive with factors and multiples.
media.description: A three-digit number is reversed and the smaller is subtracted from the larger, revealing a result that is always a multiple of nine. While one student calls it a trick and another searches for a case that breaks the pattern, a shopkeeper uses a similar divisibility rule to check a long bill for divisibility by three without dividing. The clip explores why a few examples can suggest a rule but cannot prove it, and why mathematicians look for the reason behind a pattern rather than trusting a lucky start.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Arouse curiosity about why a digit pattern holds and why a divisibility shortcut works. Key teaching points: 1) A pattern can survive every test and still need a reason. 2) A counterexample would settle it instantly, and none appears. 3) A shortcut nobody can explain is not trustworthy. 4) The chapter will supply reasons for both. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often accept a pattern as proved after a few successful cases. 2) Students often use a divisibility rule without knowing why it works. Pause points: 0:30, at the end of trick, or coincidence: ask the class to try the reversal subtraction on their own number. 1:15, just before the opening question: ask how the shopkeeper might be checking the bill. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask whether a few cases can prove a rule. After viewing, ask what a reason would look like here.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT
    Set an unbroken pattern beside an unexplained shortcut, make three agreeing cases feel
    like evidence and then feel like nothing at all, and refuse to explain either one.

  STORY
    A reversal subtraction keeps giving multiples of nine, a shopkeeper checks a bill
    instantly, and neither is explained.

  RENDERER
    Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
    1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content
    inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

  CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter
    Background: dark slate #1F2937.
    Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
    Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
    Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
    Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
    Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
    Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
    Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
    Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
    Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

  ASSETS
    No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
    from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
    NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the procedure: pick a three digit number, reverse it, and subtract the smaller from the larger
    the results shown: 742 minus 247 gives 495, and 631 minus 136 gives 495, and 852 minus 258 gives 594
    the claim: every answer is a multiple of nine
    what a few examples do: seem to shout a rule
    what one hidden case can do: break it
    the question posed: whether a pattern spotted in three tries will survive every try
    the two students: one calls it a trick, and one calls it a coincidence and hunts for the case that breaks it
    the shopkeeper: checks a long bill for divisibility by three in a couple of seconds, with no division at all, and will not say how
    the chapter's stance: testing forever is not a proof, and a shortcut nobody can explain is not much better
    why a mathematician hunts for a reason: rather than trusting a lucky start
    withheld: every method, every test and every proof, any reason, and any counterexample

  SCENE PLAN
    Total running time 90 seconds across 6 scenes.

    Scene 1. Reverse it and subtract
      Duration: 15 seconds.
      On screen at the start: an empty dark slate frame.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  Write(s1_caption) over 0.9 s, to set the frame of the scene.
      at 3.2 s  Create(s1_table) over 1.8 s, lag_ratio 0.22, to reveal the table row by row.
      at 7.0 s  FadeIn(s1_tnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 10.0 s  Indicate(s1_caption) over 0.9 s, to hold the eye on what has just appeared.
      at 12.6 s  FadeOut(s1_table, s1_tnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Pick any three digit number at all, reverse its digits, and subtract the smaller from the larger. The answer that comes back is a multiple of nine, and it keeps on being a multiple of nine."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

    Scene 2. Three tries agree
      Duration: 14 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s1_caption, s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.6 s  FadeIn(s2_chips) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.18, to bring the row in one chip at a time.
      at 5.8 s  Indicate(s2_chips) over 0.9 s, lag_ratio 0.1, to sweep across the whole row.
      at 8.4 s  FadeIn(s2_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 11.4 s  FadeOut(s2_chips, s2_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "A few examples seem to shout a rule at you. Three tries, and every single one of them agrees with the others perfectly. But one hidden case could still break it."
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

    Scene 3. Trick, or coincidence
      Duration: 15 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s2_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s2_caption, s3_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.6 s  Create(s3_panels) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.3, to open the panels one after another.
      at 5.4 s  Write(s3_paneltitles) over 1.1 s, lag_ratio 0.25, to name what each panel holds.
      at 8.0 s  FadeIn(s3_panelnotes) over 0.9 s, lag_ratio 0.25, to add the detail that was observed.
      at 10.4 s  FadeIn(s3_panelfooter) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 12.6 s  FadeOut(s3_panels, s3_paneltitles, s3_panelnotes, s3_panelfooter) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "One student calls the whole thing a trick. Another calls it a coincidence that will break eventually, and goes off hunting for the one case that finally breaks it for good."
      Persists into the next scene: s3_caption.

    Scene 4. A shopkeeper, in seconds
      Duration: 15 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s3_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s3_caption, s4_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.7 s  FadeIn(s4_sub) over 0.9 s, to state the situation.
      at 5.1 s  Indicate(s4_sub) over 0.8 s, to press on the surprising part.
      at 7.5 s  FadeIn(s4_lines) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.35, to lay the observations down one under another.
      at 10.5 s  FadeIn(s4_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 12.8 s  FadeOut(s4_sub, s4_lines, s4_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Meanwhile a shopkeeper checks a long bill for divisibility by three in a couple of seconds flat, with no division at all anywhere, and he flatly refuses to say how he manages it."
      Persists into the next scene: s4_caption.

    Scene 5. Testing is not proof
      Duration: 15 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s4_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s4_caption, s5_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 3.0 s  FadeIn(s5_chips) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.18, to bring the row in one chip at a time.
      at 6.4 s  Indicate(s5_chips) over 0.9 s, lag_ratio 0.1, to sweep across the whole row.
      at 9.4 s  FadeIn(s5_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 12.4 s  FadeOut(s5_chips, s5_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "But testing forever is simply not a proof, however many cases happen to agree, and a shortcut that nobody can explain is not really very much better than a guess."
      Persists into the next scene: s5_caption.

    Scene 6. The opening question
      Duration: 16 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s5_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  AddTextLetterByLetter(s6_question) over 1.8 s, to let the question land word by word.
      at 4.0 s  Create(s6_rule) over 0.6 s, to underline the question.
      at 6.6 s  FadeIn(s6_qsub) over 0.7 s, to name where the student will go looking.
      at 9.2 s  Circumscribe(s6_question) over 1.4 s, to hold the question as the closing image.
      at 12.6 s  Indicate(s6_question) over 0.9 s, to hold the eye on what has just appeared.
      Narration: "So will it always happen, and why should it? A mathematician hunts for a reason instead of trusting a lucky start. Line them up on the Rows and Signs Board and see."
      Persists into the next scene: nothing, this is the last scene.

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

  MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may
    pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.
    Check the three subtractions: 742 - 247 = 495, 631 - 136 = 495, 852 - 258 = 594.
    Each answer is a multiple of nine: 495 = 9 x 55 and 594 = 9 x 66. No other
    quotient, remainder or factorisation may appear on screen.

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on
    screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places
    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No rule, formula, method or answer from any later part of the chapter.
    Nothing is taught here; the film only opens questions.
    No divisibility test is stated, and no reason for the nines is given.
    No counterexample is produced, because none exists to produce.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

  SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT
    1. Scene durations sum to exactly 90 seconds across 6 scenes.
    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
    9. Nothing in the film teaches a rule or reveals a later result.
    10. The film closes on curiosity about the chapter, and the named tool is handed to the student in the closing narration.

media.title: The parity of a signed sum
labels: flipping a sign moves the value by twice that number
so the parity does not change
media.context: Placing plus and minus signs among numbers does not change whether the answer is even or odd, because flipping a sign changes the value by twice that number. The worked example asks whether 3 plus 8 minus 5 plus 6 is even or odd, decided from the plain sum. The figure compares both.
media.description: The parity of a signed sum: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'Is 3 + 8 - 5 + 6 even or odd? Use the plain sum to decide'.

source_image.alt: Diagram for the parity of a signed sum.
source_image.shows: The parity of a signed sum
source_image.caption: The parity of a signed sum: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'Is 3 + 8 - 5 + 6 even or odd? Use the plain sum to decide'.

media.teaching_notes: Compute both and ask what they have in common despite differing. The doubling argument is the reason and is worth stating carefully. Then rearrange the signs again and check the parity has not moved.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a value that is arithmetically wrong; the two parities shown as different; a sign flip described as changing the value by the number itself; a parity tag that contradicts its value; a fifth term introduced
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: Two expression rows sit one above the other. The upper, headed the signed expression, reads 3 + 8 - 5 + 6 with a value card reading 12 and an even tag. The lower, headed the plain sum, reads 3 + 8 + 5 + 6 with a value card reading 22 and an even tag. A comparison strip between them notes that the two values differ but their parity does not. Below, a sign flip note shows one term changing sign, with a strip reading that the value moves by twice that number and a tag reading that twice anything is even, so the parity cannot change. A counter row shows both parities as even, ticked. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: 3 + 8 - 5 + 6; 12; even; 3 + 8 + 5 + 6; 22; even; flipping a sign moves the value by twice that number; twice anything is even; so the parity does not change.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The signed expression must value 12 and the plain sum 22, both even.
The sign flip must be described as moving the value by twice the number.
Both parity tags must read even.
The same four numbers must appear in both rows.
Every value shown must be arithmetically correct.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

topics.summary: Runs of consecutive numbers, the parity of a signed sum, when two even numbers make a multiple of 4, and why divisibility survives adding, subtracting, and passing to factors and multiples. Each pattern is proven with rows of dots and with algebra, not settled by a few examples.

content.text:
A whole number k divides a number A when A can be split into a whole number of equal groups of size k, leaving no remainder. We then say that A is divisible by k, that k is a factor or a divisor of A, and that A is a multiple of k. These are four ways of stating one and the same fact.

A number that divides two given numbers at the same time is called a common divisor of those numbers.

The whole chapter turns on this one relation. Asking whether a sum of consecutive numbers is a multiple of something, asking whether a digit test passes, and asking whether a common divisor survives an addition are all the same question asked about different numbers.

content.text: A run of numbers that follow one after another, like 5, 6, 7, is a run of consecutive numbers. Every odd number is a sum of two consecutive numbers, because two in a row always add to an odd total. When you add an odd count of consecutive numbers, such as three or five or seven, the total is that count times the middle number, so it is a multiple of the count. An even count behaves differently: four in a row add to 2 more than a multiple of 4. The only whole numbers that cannot be written as a sum of two or more consecutive numbers are the powers of 2.

content.text: Take four numbers and put plus or minus signs between them, like a + b - c - d. However you place the signs, the answer is even or odd in exactly the same way as the plain sum a + b + c + d. The reason is that switching any one sign changes the value by twice that number, and twice a number is always even, so an even result stays even and an odd result stays odd. This means you can decide the parity of any signed form just by looking at the plain sum, without working out the value at all.

content.text: Every even number leaves either remainder 0 or remainder 2 when divided by 4. If both numbers are multiples of 4 (remainder 0), their sum is a multiple of 4. If both leave remainder 2, their two spare 2s join to make a full group of 4, so the sum is again a multiple of 4. Only the mixed case fails: a multiple of 4 added to a number that is 2 past a multiple of 4 leaves a spare 2, so the sum is not a multiple of 4. You can decide the outcome just from the remainders, without adding.

If a number is divisible by k, then it is divisible by every factor of k. The reason is that each group of k can be cut into equal factor-groups: if k = f times g, then every k-group is g smaller groups of f, so f fits exactly. Divisibility does not pass up to larger multiples of k, though: being divisible by 8 does not make a number divisible by 16. learning_objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that k divides A when A splits into whole groups of k with no remainder, and give the four equivalent phrasings using divides, divisible, factor and multiple. They will decide for a given pair whether one divides the other and name a common divisor of two given numbers.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what a run of numbers following one after another produces when they are added, and determine that an odd count of consecutive numbers totals that count times the middle number, so the sum is a multiple of the count. They will explain that every odd number is a sum of two consecutive numbers, while four in a row land 2 past a multiple of 4, so the count itself decides the pattern.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what happens to a total when plus and minus signs are placed between numbers, and determine that any signed arrangement stays even or odd in exactly the same way as the plain sum of the same numbers. They will explain that flipping one sign changes the value by twice that number, and twice any number is even, so the parity can never shift however the signs fall.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the remainders of two even numbers on division by 4 reveal about their sum, and determine that the sum is a multiple of 4 when both leave remainder 0 or both leave remainder 2, and misses only in the mixed case. They will explain that two spare 2s join into a full group of 4, while a lone spare 2 leaves the sum short, so the remainders alone decide the outcome.

media.title: Divisibility Rule Bench
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Chapter 5 Number Play, the section on checking divisibility quickly. It is read where the quick tests for 2, 4, 5, 8, 10 and 11 stop being a list to memorise: seeing which digits each rule reads is what turns them into consequences of place value. The general form is written from the units end, the rule for 11 is stated as (sum of digits in odd places) minus (sum in even places), and the phrase used for combining is 'share no common factor other than 1' — the word coprime is not used at this grade. There is no tester for 9 anywhere on this bench.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the digits each rule read.
whatYouLearned: Each divisibility rule reads only the places that are not already multiples of its divisor
The rule for 4 needs two digits and the rule for 8 needs three, for that reason

overview.goal: The student applies the correct rule for each divisor and states which part of the number that rule needs.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A bench of divisibility testers set beneath one large number, the way a row of instruments sits under the thing being measured. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A digit of the number is about to change, and the bench is asked which of its rules could possibly notice.
overview.concept: A divisibility rule reads only part of a number, and which part follows from place value. The rules for 2, 5 and 10 read the units digit; the rule for 4 reads the last two digits and the rule for 8 the last three, because 100 and 1000 are already multiples of 4 and 8. The rule for 11 reads every digit with alternating signs. Changing a digit a rule does not read cannot change its verdict.
overview.purpose: The student applies the correct rule for each divisor and states which part of the number that rule needs.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Number across the upper main panel, testers stacked beneath. On a 390 px frame the testers scroll vertically as a list while the number stays pinned above, because the highlight must stay visible. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not light any tester while a prediction is still open, and never highlight a digit a rule does not read. A false highlight would misstate the rule's scope, which is the only thing the tool teaches.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Every place from the hundreds upward is a multiple of 4, so only the last two digits can affect a remainder on division by 4. Every place from the thousands upward is a multiple of 8, so only the last three matter there. The rule reads exactly the places that are not already multiples of the divisor, which is why the highlight is not arbitrary and why a digit outside it is genuinely irrelevant. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

Each item sets the number and the divisor set from its own values, shows the question, then reveals the highlighted digits, the verdicts and the answer together as one beat. learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A rule that does not read a digit cannot be affected by changing it. Breaks: Rules applied to the wrong digits, so the scope of a rule is treated as vague. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Passing two rules does not give their product when the divisors share a factor. Breaks: Divisible by 2 and by 4 assumed to give divisible by 8. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): A rule reads exactly the places that are not already multiples of the divisor. Breaks: Divisibility rules treated as arbitrary tricks, so the digits read look like a choice. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A rule short of digits reads the whole number rather than inventing leading zeros. Breaks: Believing a rule must fail or pad with zeros when the number is too short. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Two rules combine exactly when their divisors share no common factor above 1. Breaks: Divisible by 2 and 3 assumed not to give 6, by analogy with the failure of 2 and 4.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the number on screen, every tester DARK, and asks which rules could change if the thousands digit were edited. Beat 2 lights the testers one at a time, each highlighting only the digits it reads, so the scope of each rule is visible. Beat 3 edits the thousands digit and only the testers that were reading it move, settling the prediction. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setNumber, editDigit, showTester and say.
whatYouLearned: Each divisibility rule reads only the places that are not already multiples of its divisor
The rule for 4 needs two digits and the rule for 8 needs three, for that reason
A digit a rule does not read cannot change that rule's answer
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the bench with the number on screen, every tester dark and no digit highlighted, and ask the class to name out loud which rules could change if the thousands digit were edited. Commit the class list on the prediction pad. Target the number 7316 with all six testers dark. Never light a tester before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Light the six testers one after another so each draws its bracket up to the digits it reads. Point at the bracket for 4 and then at the bracket for 8. Targets the testers 2, 4, 5, 8, 10 and 11 in that order, and read every verdict from the tool's own chips. Call 3. Edit the thousands digit and let only the testers that read it move, with the committed list held beside the result. Targets the thousands digit and the tester for 11, which is the one visible rule reading every digit. Read the list of testers that changed from the tool's own readout, never from this plan.

hunts: SILENT EDIT: change one digit so that not a single tester moves, then say why that digit was safe.
TWO PASS TRAP: find a number that passes 2 and 4 and fails 8, then one that passes 2 and 3 and passes 6.
SHORT NUMBER: put a two digit number on the bench and say what the tester for 8 reads.
ONE STEP: step the number up by one and predict which verdicts flip before you look.

observationsAndConclusions.why: A rule that reads only the last two digits has no way to notice a change in the thousands place
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Editing a digit that no tester reads leaves every verdict exactly where it was
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A rule's scope is a consequence of place value, not a convention that could have been chosen differently

observationsAndConclusions.why: 2 and 4 share the factor 2, so passing both can supply that factor twice while 8 needs it three times
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A number passes the tests for 2 and for 4 and then fails the test for 8
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Two rules do not combine into their product when their divisors share a factor

observationsAndConclusions.why: 2 and 3 share no common factor, so passing both supplies every prime that 6 needs, to full strength
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Every number that passes 2 and 3 also passes 6
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The condition for combining is about shared factors, never about the size of the divisors

media.description: A number stands across the top of the bench in separate digit cells, and beneath it a row of testers — one per divisor — each drawing a bracket up to exactly the digits its own rule reads and carrying a verdict chip beside it. The bracket and the verdict come out of the SAME pure function, so the picture can never disagree with the answer: the testers for 2, 5 and 10 reach only the units cell, the tester for 4 reaches two cells, the tester for 8 reaches three, and the tester for 11 spans every cell and prints the two place sums and their difference, with a difference of 0 read as a pass. Every bracket grows from the units end leftwards, which is the direction the rule is actually applied in. Editing a digit re-runs only the testers whose bracket contains it and marks them as moved while the rest are named as frozen, and stepping the number up or down by one recomputes the whole bench the same way. The place strip turns the scope into an argument rather than a convention: the places that are already multiples of the divisor are struck through and tagged, and only the places left over carry the bracket. Numbers that pass two rules and fail their product are kept on the bench on purpose, so the combining trap is a thing the class watches rather than a footnote.

concept.notation: Each tester is labelled with its divisor and highlights the digits it reads. A rule that reads nothing outside its highlight cannot be affected by a change outside it.
concept.statement: A divisibility rule reads only part of a number, and which part follows from place value. The rules for 2, 5 and 10 read the units digit; the rule for 4 reads the last two digits and the rule for 8 the last three, because 100 and 1000 are already multiples of 4 and 8. The rule for 11 reads every digit with alternating signs. Changing a digit a rule does not read cannot change its verdict.
prerequisites: place value and powers of ten
misconceptions: Rules applied to the wrong digits, so the rule for 4 is tried on the units digit alone.
Divisible by 2 and by 4 assumed to give divisible by 8, and divisible by 2 and 3 assumed not to give 6.
concept.why_it_is_true: Every place from the hundreds upward is a multiple of 4, so only the last two digits can affect a remainder on division by 4. Every place from the thousands upward is a multiple of 8, so only the last three matter there. The rule reads exactly the places that are not already multiples of the divisor, which is why the highlight is not arbitrary and why a digit outside it is genuinely irrelevant.
worked_numbers: For 4 the rule reads the last two digits: 7316 passes because 16 is a multiple of 4.
For 8 the rule reads the last three: 7316 fails because 316 is not a multiple of 8.
Editing the thousands digit of 7316 changes the verdicts for 11 and for 9 but not for 2, 4, 5, 8 or 10.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the class SEES the scope before it hears the rules. Six brackets of four different widths sit under one number at the same time, and the point is made by the picture: three testers reach one cell, one reaches two, one reaches three, and one spans the lot. Read the verdict chips off the tool; never quote a number from memory.

Beat 2 is the whole argument, drawn. 7316 is broken into 7000, 300, 10 and 6; the two places that are already multiples of 4 are struck through and tagged, so what is left over — 16 — is visibly the only thing that can decide. Then say the same sentence about 8 and 1000, and the two bracket widths stop being arbitrary.

Beat 3 settles it with one edit. The thousands digit goes 7 to 8 and exactly one chip moves: the tester for 11, whose difference becomes 0, which is a multiple of 11 and therefore a pass. The other five are frozen because their brackets never reached that cell. Take the class's prediction OUT LOUD before the edit and commit it with predict(); the committed list then sits beside the result.

media.title: A Number's Secret Remainder
media.context: This hook opens the topic on divisibility tests. Students can prove simple facts. The film must not state any test and must not explain why any of them works.
media.description: Without dividing at all, a glance at the digits can tell whether eight, nine or eleven fits perfectly. The clip dangles the mystery of why the last digits, the digit sum and an alternating sum each betray a number's remainder.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Use and justify the divisibility tests for two, four, eight, three, nine and eleven. Key teaching points: 1) The last digits decide divisibility by two, four and eight. 2) The digit sum decides divisibility by three and by nine. 3) An alternating sum of the digits decides divisibility by eleven. 4) Two coprime tests can be combined to test their product. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often use the digit sum test for numbers other than three and nine. 2) Students often add the digits for eleven instead of alternating the signs. Pause points: 0:24, at the end of no division anywhere: ask which test the class already knows. 0:24, just before the open question: ask why the last digits alone could settle eight. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask how they would test a long number for nine. After viewing, ask what an alternating sum could be for.

media.title: Combined Divisibility Trap
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash 'Number Play', after the individual divisibility tests for 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 and 11 are secure. The student can already apply several tests and now needs to know what applying two of them TOGETHER actually establishes. The canonical NCERT framing is the printed exercise 'a number is divisible by both 4 and 6 — must it be divisible by 4 x 6 = 24?', answered No by 12, 36 and 60. Prerequisites assumed: the divisibility rules themselves, common factors, HCF and LCM. Nothing here needs prime factorisation beyond naming the repeated factor.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the highest common factor that explains it.
whatYouLearned: Two divisibility tests give their product only when the divisors share no factor
One verified counterexample ends a combination claim

overview.goal: The student decides when two divisibility rules can be combined and produces a machine checked counterexample when they cannot.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A claim written across the top of a working surface with a strip of numbers beneath it, the way a statement on the board sits above the numbers used to test it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A claim says that passing two divisibility tests gives the third, and a single number from the strip is allowed to end it.
overview.concept: Passing the tests for two divisors gives divisibility by their product only when the two divisors share no common factor. 2 and 4 share the factor 2, so passing both says less than it looks and 12 breaks the claim. 2 and 3 share nothing, so passing both really does give 6.
overview.purpose: The student decides when two divisibility rules can be combined and produces a machine checked counterexample when they cannot.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Claim top, strip centre, verdict card beneath. Contrast panel to the right on a wide frame and below the verdicts on a 390 px frame. Every strip number keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show whether the combination holds while a prediction is still open, and never accept a counterexample without verifying it. An unverified counterexample teaches that naming a number is testing it.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. If a and b share a factor, then a number can satisfy both while carrying that shared factor only once, which is not enough for the product. 12 has 2 twice, which satisfies 2 and 4, but 8 needs three twos. When a and b share nothing, satisfying both forces every prime of a and every prime of b to be present to full strength, and those requirements do not overlap, so the product follows. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A divisor of 1 is the boundary case of the coprime condition, and the claim holds there. Breaks: Believing every combination claim must have a counterexample somewhere. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): When one divisor divides the other, passing both says no more than passing the larger. Breaks: A working pair taken as evidence that all pairs combine. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Two divisors combine exactly when they share no common factor above 1. Breaks: Divisibility rules combined by multiplying the divisors regardless of shared factors. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): An empty search becomes a result only when the coprime condition explains it. Breaks: Reading an empty search as a failure to look hard enough. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A rule read off the demonstrated cases must survive a pair it was not built from. Breaks: A working pair taken as evidence that all pairs combine.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the claim on screen and the verdict HIDDEN, and asks whether dividing by 2 and by 4 must give 8. Beat 2 pulls 12 off the strip, which divides by 2 and by 4 and not by 8, so the claim falls to one number. Beat 3 puts the working pair beside it, 2 and 3 giving 6, and asks what is different about the two pairs. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setClaim, testNumber, showContrast and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with the claim for 2 and 4 written across the top, an untouched strip and no verdict anywhere, and ask the class to answer yes or no out loud and give a reason. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the pair 2 and 4 with nothing tested. Never test a number before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Pull 12 out of the strip and test it, so the three verdict chips fill left to right as two passes and one failure. Point at the third chip. Target the number 12 against the pair 2 and 4, and read all three verdicts from the tool's own chips. Call 3. Put the pair 2 and 3 beside it in the contrast panel and let the two highest common factors appear last, then ask what is different about the pairs. Targets the contrast pair 2 and 3 and the two highest common factor badges, both read from the tool rather than from this plan.

hunts: COUNTEREXAMPLE RACE: pick a pair with a shared factor and find three different counterexamples.
EMPTY SEARCH: pick a coprime pair, sweep the whole strip, and say why the search had to come up empty.
NESTED PAIR: set a pair where one divisor divides the other and say what passing both really tells you.
STATE YOUR RULE: type a condition for combining and test it on a pair you did not use to build it.

media.description: A combination claim is written across the top of a working surface — divides by a AND divides by b, therefore divides by a x b — and a strip of numbers runs beneath it. Tapping any number on the strip returns three verdicts at once, by the first divisor, by the second and by their product, so a counterexample is recognised as a PATTERN of two passes and one failure rather than as a number somebody remembered. A submitted counterexample is machine verified and, when it is not one, returned with the test it failed; a sweep of the whole strip for a pair that shares no factor comes back with two separate lines — what was searched, and then why nothing can exist anywhere — so an empty search becomes a reason instead of a shrug. A proportional mini rail marks every counterexample in the whole range at once, and a contrast panel puts a second claim beside the first so the two behave differently on the same strip. The highest common factor of each pair is printed only AFTER that contrast has been watched, so the deciding quantity arrives as an explanation and never as a rule handed out first. Concept runs three teaching beats; Learn walks the five reviewed checkpoints already answered; Practice serves six drawn questions on a difficulty ladder with a star finish and a Review pass; Free Play unlocks the divisor pair, the strip length, the sweep, the counterexample check and a typed rule that the tool tests on a pair it was not built from.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the combination claim from its own divisors, shows the question, then reveals the counterexample or the confirmation and the reason together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the claim on screen and the verdict HIDDEN, and asks whether dividing by 2 and by 4 must give 8. Beat 2 pulls 12 off the strip, which divides by 2 and by 4 and not by 8, so the claim falls to one number. Beat 3 puts the working pair beside it, 2 and 3 giving 6, and asks what is different about the two pairs. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setClaim, testNumber, showContrast and say.

concept.notation: A combination claim is written as divisible by a and by b means divisible by a times b. The highest common factor of a and b is written as their HCF.
concept.statement: Passing the tests for two divisors gives divisibility by their product only when the two divisors share no common factor. 2 and 4 share the factor 2, so passing both says less than it looks and 12 breaks the claim. 2 and 3 share nothing, so passing both really does give 6.
misconceptions: Divisibility rules combined by multiplying the divisors regardless of shared factors.
A working pair taken as evidence that all pairs combine.
concept.why_it_is_true: If a and b share a factor, then a number can satisfy both while carrying that shared factor only once, which is not enough for the product. 12 has 2 twice, which satisfies 2 and 4, but 8 needs three twos. When a and b share nothing, satisfying both forces every prime of a and every prime of b to be present to full strength, and those requirements do not overlap, so the product follows.
worked_numbers: 12 divides by 2 and by 4 but not by 8, so the claim for 2 and 4 fails.
20 does the same, so counterexamples are not rare.
12 divides by 2 and by 3 and by 6, and every number that passes 2 and 3 passes 6, because their HCF is 1.

answer_key.worked: Two rules combine to their product exactly when the divisors share no common factor. 2 and 4 share a factor, so 12 breaks the claim; 2 and 3 share none, so 6 follows.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn claim: whether the combination holds, the highest common factor of the pair, and whether a submitted counterexample genuinely breaks it.
answer_key.precision: Counterexamples are found by search over a bounded range rather than from a hard coded list, so any valid number is accepted. Exact integer arithmetic throughout.
answer_key.ground_truth: hcf(a, b) = the Euclidean algorithm. combinationHolds(a, b) = hcf(a, b) is 1. counterexamples(a, b) = every n in the searched range divisible by a and by b but not by a times b.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the claim falls to ONE number in front of the class. The three chips fill left to right — pass, pass, fail — and the third chip contradicts the rule the student is silently applying, which is 'multiply the divisors'. Never announce that 12 is a counterexample; let the pattern be the announcement, and ask the class out loud, before the beat, whether passing 2 and 4 must give 8.

Beat 2 answers the question the counterexample raises: WHY was one number enough? The prime bricks show 12 carrying the factor 2 twice while 8 demands it three times, and the strip's rail fills with 25 more counterexamples up to 200, so this is a pattern and not a lucky number. Keep the HCF off the screen here — it has not been earned yet.

Beat 3 is where the deciding quantity finally arrives. The two claims sit on the SAME strip, so the difference cannot be blamed on the numbers tested, and only then do the two HCF badges appear: 2 for the pair that breaks, 1 for the pair that holds. Say 'shares no common factor apart from 1' beside 'HCF is 1' — the words carry the meaning that the abbreviation only labels.

topics.summary: The quick tests for 2, 4, 8, 9, 3, and 11, digital roots, and combining coprime factors for 6, 12, and 24, each justified by the remainder every place value leaves. A number's units digit alone cannot decide divisibility by 9, and the digit-sum and alternating-sum tests are consequences of place value, not tricks.

content.text: To test for 2, look only at the units digit: the number is divisible by 2 when that digit is even. To test for 4, look at the last two digits; to test for 8, look at the last three digits. The reason is place value. Every place from tens upward is a multiple of 10, and 10 is a multiple of 2. Every place from hundreds upward is a multiple of 100, and 100 is a multiple of 4. Every place from thousands upward is a multiple of 1000, and 1000 is a multiple of 8. So those higher places fall into full groups and leave no remainder, and only the final digits decide.

content.text: A number is divisible by 9 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 9, and divisible by 3 when the digit sum is divisible by 3. The reason is that each place value is one more than a multiple of both 9 and 3: 10 = 9 + 1, 100 = 99 + 1, 1000 = 999 + 1. So each digit brings a whole multiple-of-9 part plus the digit itself, and only the sum of the digits is left over. If that digit sum is a multiple of 9 (or of 3), so is the number. Note that a number can pass the 3-test yet fail the 9-test, because not every multiple of 3 is a multiple of 9.

content.text: To test for 11, add and subtract the digits in turn, starting from the units: units plus, tens minus, hundreds plus, thousands minus, and so on. The number is divisible by 11 when this alternating total is 0 or a multiple of 11. The reason is that place values alternate around multiples of 11: 1 and 100 and 10000 are each one more than a multiple of 11, while 10 and 1000 are each one less. The one-more places add their digit and the one-less places take theirs away, so the alternating digit sum is exactly the remainder pattern for 11.

content.text: The digital root of a number is found by adding its digits, then adding the digits of that result, and so on until a single digit is left. For example, 7284 gives 7 + 2 + 8 + 4 = 21, then 2 + 1 = 3, so its digital root is 3. This single digit is exactly the remainder the number leaves on division by 9, because each folding step keeps the mod-9 remainder unchanged. The one exception in wording is a multiple of 9, whose digital root shows as 9 even though the remainder is 0. Digital roots add and multiply like remainders, so they give a quick check on arithmetic.

content.text:
Two numbers whose only common factor is 1, that is whose HCF is 1, are called co-prime numbers. So 3 and 8 are co-prime, and so are 4 and 9, even though neither pair is made of primes.

Two numbers can be co-prime without either being prime, and two numbers can both be composite and still fail to be co-prime. Only the shared factors decide it.

The idea matters here because divisibility tests may be combined only across co-prime factors. A number divisible by both 3 and 8 is divisible by 24, since 3 and 8 are co-prime, but a number divisible by both 4 and 6 need not be divisible by 24, because 4 and 6 share the factor 2.

content.text: To test divisibility by a number that splits into two factors, you can check each factor separately, but only if the two factors share no common factor. Then passing both forces divisibility by their product. For 6, use 2 and 3. For 12, use 3 and 4. For 24, use 3 and 8. The pair 4 and 6 does not work for 24, because 4 and 6 share the factor 2, so passing both only forces their LCM, which is 12. When two divisors share a factor, that factor is counted only once, so their combined guarantee is the LCM, not the product.

topics.brief_summary: The quick tests for 2, 4, 8, 9, 3, and 11, digital roots, and combining coprime factors for 6, 12, and 24, each justified by the remainder every place value leaves. A number's units digit alone cannot decide divisibility by 9, and the digit-sum and alternating-sum tests are consequences of place value, not tricks.
topics.original_chunk: To test for 2, look only at the units digit: the number is divisible by 2 when that digit is even. To test for 4, look at the last two digits; to test for 8, look at the last three digits. The reason is place value. Every place from tens upward is a multiple of 10, and 10 is a multiple of 2. Every place from hundreds upward is a multiple of 100, and 100 is a multiple of 4. Every place from thousands upward is a multiple of 1000, and 1000 is a multiple of 8. So those higher places fall into full groups and leave no remainder, and only the final digits decide. Worked examples of last-digit tests for 2, 4, and 8, demonstrated one step at a time across different cases. learning_objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the closing digits of a number decide about divisibility by 2, 4, and 8, and determine that the units digit settles 2, the last two digits settle 4, and the last three digits settle 8. They will explain that place value is the reason, since 10 is a multiple of 2, 100 a multiple of 4, and 1000 a multiple of 8, so every higher place drops out cleanly.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the sum of a number's digits reveals about divisibility by 9 and by 3, and determine that a number is divisible by 9 or by 3 exactly when its digit sum is. They will explain that each place value sits one above a multiple of 9 and of 3, so every digit leaves only itself behind, and that a number can pass the 3 test yet fail the 9 test.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what an alternating add and subtract of the digits reveals about divisibility by 11, and determine that a number is divisible by 11 when this alternating total is 0 or a multiple of 11. They will explain that place values sit one above or one below a multiple of 11 in turn, so the plus and minus signs track those gaps and only their alternating sum is left over.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what folding a number's digits down to a single digit produces, and determine that this digital root equals the remainder the number leaves on division by 9. They will explain that each folding step keeps the mod 9 remainder unchanged, so the final single digit carries it, with the one wording exception that a multiple of 9 shows a digital root of 9 while its true remainder is 0.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that two numbers with no common factor other than 1 are called co-prime, and that two divisibility tests may be combined only when the two divisors are co-prime. They will decide whether a given pair is co-prime and say which pairs of tests may be combined to test a given divisor.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what testing two separate factors decides about divisibility by their product, and determine that passing both forces divisibility only when the two factors share no common factor. They will explain that 6 splits into 2 and 3 and 24 into 3 and 8, while 4 and 6 fail for 24 because their shared factor of 2 is counted once, so their combined guarantee reaches only 12.

A reasoning column runs to the right in three steps: the units column is T plus T plus T, which is three T and must end in the digit T; the digits satisfying this are listed and 0 is struck out because T is a leading letter, leaving T equal to 5; a substitution then runs the whole sum as 55 plus 55 plus 55 equal to 165, filling F equal to 1 and U equal to 6. A rules card at the side reads that two different letters never share a digit and a leading letter is never 0, and a check strip reads '55 x 3 = 165'. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: T T; T T; T T; F U T; the units column; three T must end in T; T = 5; a leading letter is never 0; 55 + 55 + 55 = 165; F = 1; U = 6.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The reasoning must start at the units column and must justify T equal to 5.
T must not be 0, since it is a leading letter.
The substitution must read 55 plus 55 plus 55 equal to 165, giving F equal to 1 and U equal to 6.
No two letters may share a digit.
The check must confirm 55 times 3 equals 165.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Digit Puzzle Solver
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.5 Number Play, section 5.3 Digits in Disguise. The printed rules are reproduced in the textbook's own words: each letter stands for one digit, the same digit wherever it appears; each digit is represented by at most one letter; the first digit of a number is never 0. The figure follows the Indian notebook convention — right-aligned addends, the plus at the left of the last addend, a rule beneath it, and carries as small digits above the column they enter. Letters are capitals, one glyph per cell inside the column grid, so A B reads as place value and never as A times B, which matters in the very year the class is meeting algebra. The tool assumes column addition with carrying and place value and re-teaches neither.

overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A vertical addition written with letters in place of digits, a carry row above it and a tray of digits beneath, the way a puzzle is set out in a notebook. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: Every letter hides a digit, and the class is asked to fix one of them without trying a single assignment.
overview.concept: A cryptarithm is solved by constraints, not by trying every assignment. Two rules always hold: different letters take different digits, and a leading letter is never 0. Working column by column from the units, each column plus its incoming carry fixes what is possible, and in an addition of two numbers the carry out of any column can only be 0 or 1.
overview.purpose: The student uses place value and carrying constraints to deduce digits rather than testing all options, and explains one deduction in words.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Addition centred in the main panel with the carry row above and the digit tray below. Notes panel to the right on a wide frame and collapsed to an expandable strip beneath on a 390 px frame. Every letter cell keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not name a wrong letter, and do not reveal any digit while a prediction is still open. Naming the letter would replace the deduction with a correction.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The largest sum in a column of two digits plus an incoming carry is 9 plus 9 plus 1, which is 19, so the carry out is at most 1. That single fact fixes a leading letter created by a carry to be 1 immediately. Each column is then a small equation in the letters it contains plus a known carry, and solving those in order is far shorter than searching, which is why the tool reports the failing column rather than the failing letter. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A leading letter is never 0, because that would change the length of the number. Breaks: Ignoring carries, and allowing a leading zero. ML2 (Medium, Conceptual): The carry out of a column of two digits never exceeds 1, which fixes a new leading letter at once. Breaks: Ignoring carries, so the leading letter is searched for rather than deduced. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): Distinct letters take distinct digits, which is what makes each placement informative. Breaks: Treating letters as labels that may repeat, so a placement rules nothing out. ML4 (Hard, Conceptual): The failing column is the evidence; finding the failing letter inside it is the reasoning. Breaks: Trial and error without using the constraints, so feedback is used in place of deduction. ML5 (Hard, Edge Case): A puzzle without a unique solution is flagged, never graded as though one answer were the only one. Breaks: Assuming every digit puzzle has exactly one answer.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the puzzle and every letter empty, and asks which digit a named letter definitely cannot be. Beat 2 places a digit that follows from the ones column and that column turns green, with the carry shown above the next one. Beat 3 uses the leading letter and the fact that a carry cannot exceed one to fix it, so a deduction rather than a search does the work. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeDigit, showCarry, checkColumns and say. No drag: the agent places a digit by naming the letter.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the puzzle with every letter empty, no column green and the carry row blank, and ask the class to name out loud one digit a stated letter definitely cannot be, with a reason. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the units column of the opening puzzle. Never place a digit before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Place the digit that follows from the units column and let that column turn green with its carry travelling to the next. Point at the carry as it moves. Target the units column and its outgoing carry, and read every value from the tool's own grid. Call 3. Ask why the leading letter can only be 1, then place it and let the column verdicts follow. Targets the leading letter and the digit 1. Never name a wrong letter; name the failing column instead and let the class find the letter.

hunts: UNITS FIRST: solve a puzzle using only the units column and the carry, and see how far that alone gets you.
BREAK A RULE: try a leading zero and a repeated digit on purpose, and read the two refusals.
CARRY HUNT: build a puzzle whose total has one more digit than the addends, and say what its leading letter must be.
EXPLAIN ONE: solve any puzzle, then write the single deduction you are surest of.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each column is a small equation in its own letters plus a known carry, so it can be judged on its own
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A column turns green as soon as its letters and its incoming carry agree, before any other column is touched
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Working column by column from the units is far shorter than searching, because each column removes options for the rest

observationsAndConclusions.why: The carry out of two digits plus an incoming carry is at most 1, since 9 plus 9 plus 1 is 19
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A total with one more digit than the numbers added fixes its leading letter immediately
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A single bound on the carry settles a letter with no trial and no error at all

observationsAndConclusions.why: Different letters stand for different digits, and a leading zero would change how many digits the number has
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A repeated digit and a leading zero both spring back with the rule named
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The two standing rules are what make each placement informative rather than a guess

media.description: A cryptarithm is written the way it is written in a notebook: two addends stacked right-aligned with letters standing in for digits, a plus at the left of the last addend, a rule under it, the total below, and the carries as small digits above the column each one ENTERS. The student picks a digit and taps a letter, and it fills everywhere that letter appears — subject to two standing rules the tool enforces at the point of the attempt rather than in a preamble: no two letters may hold the same digit, and no leading letter may be 0. A refused duplicate springs back and lights BOTH letters in every cell they occupy; a refused leading zero springs back beside a ghost of the same number drawn one column SHORT, so what the class sees change is the LENGTH of the number, which is the actual reason. Every column that can be judged fills behind its digits and its outgoing carry travels visibly to the top of the next column, so the chain is a movement rather than a notation. When an assignment is wrong the tool names the failing COLUMN and never the failing letter, so finding which letter in that column cannot fit stays the student's work. A notes strip records digits the student has ruled out by reasoning, against each letter, and the checker never reads it.

mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the puzzle and every letter empty, and asks which digit a named letter definitely cannot be. Beat 2 places a digit that follows from the ones column and that column turns green, with the carry shown above the next one. Beat 3 uses the leading letter and the fact that a carry cannot exceed one to fix it, so a deduction rather than a search does the work. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeDigit, showCarry, checkColumns and say. No drag: the agent places a digit by naming the letter.

concept.notation: Each letter stands for one digit, the same digit everywhere it appears. A carry is written above the column it enters and is always 0 or 1 in an addition of two numbers.
concept.statement: A cryptarithm is solved by constraints, not by trying every assignment. Two rules always hold: different letters take different digits, and a leading letter is never 0. Working column by column from the units, each column plus its incoming carry fixes what is possible, and in an addition of two numbers the carry out of any column can only be 0 or 1.
misconceptions: Trial and error without using the constraints, so every assignment is tested in turn.
Ignoring carries, and allowing a leading zero.
concept.why_it_is_true: The largest sum in a column of two digits plus an incoming carry is 9 plus 9 plus 1, which is 19, so the carry out is at most 1. That single fact fixes a leading letter created by a carry to be 1 immediately. Each column is then a small equation in the letters it contains plus a known carry, and solving those in order is far shorter than searching, which is why the tool reports the failing column rather than the failing letter.
worked_numbers: A leading letter produced by a carry must be 1, because a carry cannot exceed one.
In the units column, the sum of the two letters ends in the answer's units digit, which rules out most digits at once.
Two different letters can never take the same digit, so each placement removes a digit from every other letter.

answer_key.precision: Solved by constraint propagation at load time to confirm uniqueness. The carry chain is checked explicitly column by column and never inferred from the final total.
answer_key.ground_truth: columnConsistent(i, assignment) = the column sum plus its incoming carry matches the answer digit and produces the stated outgoing carry. solution = the letter to digit map found by constraint propagation. isUnique = whether propagation found exactly one.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 is the definition, shown rather than asserted. The puzzle is on screen with every letter empty, the two standing rules sit beside it, and the ghost of the same total drawn one column short is what says WHY a leading letter cannot be 0 — the number would stop being a three digit number. Ask the class out loud which digit a named letter definitely cannot be, and commit their answer with predict(); never place a digit before that.

Beat 2 is the whole justification in one picture, and it is the beat that breaks the commonest error on this topic. The worst possible column is drawn live — 9 and 9 with an incoming carry of 1 — the total 19 forms, and only the 1 detaches and travels to the next column while the 9 stays. Say the qualifier every time: this is an addition of TWO numbers. Section 5.3 also prints ON + ON + ON and QR + QR + QR, where three addends push the carry to 2, and a class that carries an unqualified rule into that exercise is stuck.

Beat 3 spends the bound. The leading column of A B + C A = B B C holds nothing but the carry, so B is 1 by deduction and not by search; A and C then follow from the units and tens columns and all three columns turn green from the units end. Point at the carry as it travels. Read every number off the tool's own grid, from state.truth, and never from your own arithmetic.

media.description: Each letter secretly stands for one digit, and yet the sum still has to add up. The clip invites the student to crack a coded addition from its units column, where careful reasoning pins every letter with no guessing at all.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Solve addition and multiplication cryptarithms by reasoning from the units column. Key teaching points: 1) Each letter stands for exactly one digit and each digit for one letter. 2) The units column receives no carry, so it is the safest start. 3) A carry out of a column is at most one. 4) Divisibility and place value narrow the possibilities further. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often start at the leftmost column where the carry is unknown. 2) Students often allow two letters to take the same digit. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of start at the units: ask which column the class would start from. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what the largest possible carry is. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what makes the units column special. After viewing, ask how many different digits the puzzle needs.

topics.summary: Cryptarithms where each letter is a distinct digit and no leading digit is 0. Addition puzzles are cracked from the units column and its carry, and multiplication puzzles from the units digit and the size of the product, so the solution is reasoned out rather than guessed.

content.text: A cryptarithm is a puzzle where each letter stands for a digit. Two rules always hold: two different letters never share a digit, and a leading letter is never 0. The best way to solve an addition puzzle is to start at the units column, because it depends on nothing to its right. The units letters fix the last digit of the answer and any carry into the next column, and that carry then drives the column to its left. Working column by column along the carries, each letter is pinned by reasoning, not by trying combinations at random.

Worked examples of solving addition cryptarithms, demonstrated one step at a time across different cases. A cryptarithm is a puzzle where each letter stands for a digit. Two rules always hold: two different letters never share a digit, and a leading letter is never 0. The best way to solve an addition puzzle is to start at the units column, because it depends on nothing to its right. The units letters fix the last digit of the answer and any carry into the next column, and that carry then drives the column to its left. Working column by column along the carries, each letter is pinned by reasoning, not by trying combinations at random. In a multiplication cryptarithm a two-digit number times a small number gives a hidden result, and each letter is a distinct digit with no leading 0. Start with the units digit: the units digits multiplied must end in the puzzle's units letter, which narrows the choices sharply. Next use the size of the product: the number of digits it shows limits how big the leading letter can be, since a large leader would overflow into an extra digit. Repeated letters in the result give further checks. Working from these constraints, the digits follow by deduction rather than by guessing. media.title: From a Trick to a Reason
media.context: This is the chapter summary and it plays after the final topic. Every claim it makes has already been taught and practised, so nothing new appears and no fresh number is tested. Its job is to show that place value explained every trick in the chapter.
media.description: The film gathers the chapter together with an “always, sometimes, or never true?” challenge, asking students to defend claims about factors and multiples with a reason or a single counterexample. It then shows how writing numbers by their place values turns these tricks into algebra, revealing why reversal subtraction always produces a multiple of nine: the place values differ by multiples of nine.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Restate how place value algebra explains the reversal pattern and every divisibility test. Key teaching points: 1) Any number can be written by its place values. 2) The reversal difference is a multiple of nine because the place values differ by nines. 3) The digit sum test for three and nine follows from the same argument. 4) The last digits alone settle two, four, five and eight. 5) An alternating sum settles eleven. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often keep the tests as separate memorised rules. 2) Students often think the reversal pattern is a coincidence. Pause points: 0:30, at the end of why the nines appear: ask why nine appears in the reversal difference. 1:13, just before from a trick to a reason: ask which of the four cards they would explain first. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what writing a number by its places gives you. After viewing, ask why the last digits can settle divisibility by eight.

    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
