overview.goal: The student builds a prime factorisation by any route and observes that the final set of primes is always the same.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A branching tree with the number at the top and every split drawn as two descending branches, the way a factor tree is drawn out on paper. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: Two students split the same number in different orders, and the tree is asked whether they can possibly end up with different primes.
overview.concept: Any number greater than 1 can be split into primes, and however the splitting is done the final collection of primes is the same, including how many times each appears. Only the shape of the tree changes with the route, never its leaves.
overview.purpose: The student builds a prime factorisation by any route and observes that the final set of primes is always the same.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.

Every node keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not gold a composite leaf, and never show the exponent form before every leaf is prime. A gold composite would say the factorisation was finished when it was not.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. titleFraming.normal: Free Play · Prime Factor Tree Builder

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Every split replaces a node by two factors whose product is that node, so the product of all leaves never changes and always equals the original number. Splitting can only stop at primes, and any two ways of reaching an all prime collection with the same product must use the same primes the same number of times. That is the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, met here as an observation rather than proved. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): A prime root is a finished tree, not a tree waiting for a split. Breaks: Believing every tree must have at least one split before it can be finished. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): The route changes the shape of the tree and never its leaves. Breaks: Belief that different split orders give different factorisations. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A correct product is not a finished tree; every leaf has to be prime as well. Breaks: Leaves left composite because the running product still checks out. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Sameness of factorisation is sameness of the leaf collection, including how often each prime appears. Breaks: Reading a different tree shape as a different factorisation.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the root with no splits made and no leaf gold, and ask the class to say out loud whether a different first split could end at a different collection of primes. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the root 72 unsplit. Never split a node before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Build one tree down to gold leaves and point at the running product after each split, which never moves. Target the first split 8 times 9, and read the running product and the leaves from the tool's own readouts. Call 3. Build a second tree from a different first split and let the two leaf collections pair off one for one. Targets the first split 2 times 36 and the comparison of the two collections, with the exponent form read from getState().truth.

DEEPEST TREE: find the number under 200 whose tree has the most leaves.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each split writes a node as two factors whose product is that node, so the product across the leaves never changes
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The running product beside the tree stays at the root value through every single split
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The tree is a rearrangement of one number, which is why the leaves cannot come out different

observationsAndConclusions.why: Both routes end at all prime leaves with the same product, and there is only one such collection
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Two trees grown from different first splits pair off leaf for leaf
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The shape of the tree is a choice; the collection of leaves is not

observationsAndConclusions.why: Splitting can stop only at a prime, and a composite leaf still has a split available to it
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A leaf left composite stays ungolded and the exponent form refuses to appear
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: An unfinished tree is a fact about the leaves, not about how tidy the drawing looks

media.description: A factor tree grows downwards from one number: the student taps any composite leaf, types two factors, and the split is refused unless the two multiply back to that node, so the invariant is enforced where the mistake is made rather than at the end. A prime leaf fills gold with one pulse and stops being tappable; a composite leaf keeps the indigo fill and stays open. The running product sits beside the tree and never moves, because every split replaces a node by two factors whose product is that node. The exponent form refuses to appear until every leaf is gold, so a tree whose leaves multiply back correctly but still hold a composite is visibly unfinished. Typing 1 as a factor draws the branch for a beat - the other side is seen holding the same number again - and is then refused with the textbook's own reason, that 1 is neither prime nor composite. Building a second tree from a different first split puts the two side by side and compares them on the collection of leaves rather than the shape, so two visibly different drawings are reported as agreeing.

Split a number to primes, write the exponent form, or say whether two routes give the same primes. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's tree, a correct tree and the leaf set that settles it.

theme.premise: Two students split the same number in different orders, and the tree is asked whether they can possibly end up with different primes
theme.setting: A branching tree with the number at the top and every split drawn as two descending branches, the way a factor tree is drawn out on paper
theme.visualStyle: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration
theme.studentPalette: The warmer accent of the same family, with the score and the Finish button carrying it
theme.teacherPalette: The cool indigo accent, low chrome, high contrast, so a projected board stays readable

practice.rating: all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1, never 0
practice.review: The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's tree, a correct tree, and the leaf set that explains it.

scenes.onScreen: The tree, the running product, the leaf collection, every control, no score and no question. 72 at the root with every node splittable and every control live.

scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: A tree splits a number into two factors and continues until every leaf is prime. The exponent form collects equal leaves, for example 72 as 2 cubed times 3 squared.
concept.statement: Any number greater than 1 can be split into primes, and however the splitting is done the final collection of primes is the same, including how many times each appears. Only the shape of the tree changes with the route, never its leaves.
misconceptions: Belief that different split orders give different factorisations.
Leaves left composite, and 1 written as a prime factor.
concept.why_it_is_true: Every split replaces a node by two factors whose product is that node, so the product of all leaves never changes and always equals the original number. Splitting can only stop at primes, and any two ways of reaching an all prime collection with the same product must use the same primes the same number of times. That is the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, met here as an observation rather than proved.
worked_numbers: 72 split as 2 times 36 gives the same five leaves in a different order.
The exponent form is 2 cubed times 3 squared either way.

extra: Breaking a packing count into equal boxes and then into equal rows inside a box
Splitting a rectangle's area into two whole side lengths and splitting each of those again
Reducing a fraction by pulling out shared prime factors one at a time
Cutting a length into two whole parts and cutting each part again until nothing splits
Sorting a bag of counters into equal heaps and re-sorting each heap from a different first choice
Dividing a music bar into halves and then into thirds, in either order
textbook: The printed prime factorisation used to decide which divisibility checks are enough for a larger divisor
The printed argument that a number's prime factorisation must carry the primes of each divisor to full strength
The printed nested diagrams of multiples of 4, 8 and 32, read as repeated factors of one prime
The printed statement that a number divisible by a given number is divisible by every factor of it

answer_key.worked: 72 is 2 cubed times 3 squared however it is split, because every split preserves the product and splitting can only stop at primes.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn tree: the leaf multiset, the exponent form, and whether two trees agree.
answer_key.precision: Every split is validated by exact integer multiplication. The exponent form is built from the leaf multiset, never from a stored answer.
answer_key.ground_truth: leaves(tree) = the multiset of leaf values. isComplete(tree) = every leaf is prime. exponentForm(leaves) = the prime to exponent map and its canonical string. product(leaves) = must equal the root at every moment.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Rejected with an explanatory message, because splitting off a 1 never terminates and 1 is not prime.
It is already a leaf and turns gold immediately. The tool says the tree is finished rather than waiting for a split that cannot happen.

edge_cases.case: A split whose factors do not multiply back
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Refused at entry with the product shown, so the invariant is enforced at the point of the mistake.
Stays ungolded and the tool says the tree is not finished, naming which leaves can still be split.
The leaf multisets are compared, not the tree shapes, so different shapes with the same leaves are reported as agreeing.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later.
hostProps.device: mobile / web / smartboard. Lay out for the 390 px frame first.
hostProps.questions: TOP LEVEL. The Practice bank the platform drew for this concept, from question_bank_v2 where delivery_mode = 'Practice'. Read it as props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions, top level first. When it is non empty it REPLACES the authored practice bank.
hostProps.initialMode: The mode the tool must open in, fully set up, first beat ready.
hostProps.enabledModes: Which of the four modes exist this session.
hostProps.learnQuestions: TOP LEVEL. The Learn bank for this concept, from question_bank_v2 where delivery_mode = 'Learn', mandatory checkpoints first. Read it as props.learnQuestions ?? props.additionalProps?.learnQuestions. When it is non empty those items ARE the Learn steps; the authored scene examples are only the fallback for a thin pool.
hostProps.showModeSelector: false in production for every maths tool. Honour it, defaulting to true (const showSelector = props.showModeSelector ?? true) so the selector still works in preview and review, and disappears live.
hostProps.additionalProps.exampleSeed: A 32 bit int the tool's mulberry32 PRNG consumes directly. The teacher agent builds its own copy of the example set from the SAME seed, so Math.random(), Date.now() or ignoring the seed desynchronises the narration from the screen in every single session.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'factorise', n:number} | {kind:'exponent_form', n:number} | {kind:'compare_routes', n:number, firstSplitA:number, firstSplitB:number} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

startingNumber.description: The number at the root of the tree, clamped 2 to 1000.

showRunningProduct.description: Show the product of all current leaves, which never changes and is the invariant the tool rests on.

constraints: The product of all leaves always equals the original number, checked after every split, so the invariant is enforced rather than assumed.
Every split is validated by exact integer multiplication, and 1 is rejected as a factor with an explanatory message.
The tree is a nested state object rendered recursively, so any node can be split or undone without rebuilding the whole tree.
The exponent form is derived from the leaf multiset, so it cannot disagree with the tree on screen.
Two trees are compared by leaf multiset and never by shape, because the shape is exactly what is allowed to differ.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The tree, the running product, the leaf collection, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: 72 sits unsplit at the root and no leaves are shown. The class commits whether a different first split gives the same primes, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Build: one tree is split down to gold leaves while the running product stays at 72 throughout.

animations: Split: two branches grow down from the node over 220 ms and the node stays put, so the route is recorded rather than replaced.
Gold: a leaf that turns out prime fills gold with one pulse, so finishing a branch is an event.
Compare: the two leaf collections slide together and matching primes pair off, which makes sameness a visible matching rather than a claim.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The two routes have to be built and matched leaf for leaf before the uniqueness is stated, or the result is an assertion the student has no way to doubt and therefore no way to believe

mathematical_facts: Every split writes a node as two factors whose product is that node, so the product of the leaves always equals the root
Splitting can stop only at a prime, so a composite leaf means the tree is unfinished
However the splitting is done, the final collection of primes is the same, counting repeats

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the number out of the question text and set it as the root, making no splits. If the question names a first split, apply only that one. The tree drawn must be able to reach every prime the question mentions.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.

secondTree, when the question compares two routes
question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no number in it ('why does the route not change the primes?') has nothing to split. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool 72 built two ways with both leaf collections paired off against each other, rather than fabricating a scene the question does not describe.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the guess public before any evidence arrives. 72 sits unsplit and the class is asked out loud whether starting at 8 x 9 rather than 2 x 36 could end at a different collection of primes. Commit their answer with predict() and split nothing first - the whole beat is worth one turn only because the guess is still open.

Beat 2 is the invariant made watchable. One route runs down to five gold leaves while the running product beside the tree stays on 72 through every single split. Point at the product after each split rather than at the leaves: the number that never moves is the argument, and the exponent form landing at the end is only its receipt.

Beat 3 is the refutation. The second tree is a visibly different shape reaching the same five leaves, and the verdict chip says so in words - same leaves, different shapes. Let the class find the pairing themselves: 2 with 2, 2 with 2, 2 with 2, 3 with 3, 3 with 3, and nothing left over on either side.

Compare the two trees and match the leaves one for one. 8. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

content.text: Every number greater than 1 can be split into prime factors, and however you choose to split it the final collection of primes is always the same, including how many times each one appears. Splitting 72 as 8 times 9 and splitting it as 2 times 36 give different looking trees, but both end with the leaves 2, 2, 2, 3, 3. The reason is that every split replaces a number by two factors whose product is that number, so the product of all the leaves never changes, and splitting can only stop when every leaf is prime.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that k divides A when A splits into whole groups of k with no remainder, and give the four equivalent phrasings using divides, divisible, factor and multiple. They will decide for a given pair whether one divides the other and name a common divisor of two given numbers.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what a run of numbers following one after another produces when they are added, and determine that an odd count of consecutive numbers totals that count times the middle number, so the sum is a multiple of the count. They will explain that every odd number is a sum of two consecutive numbers, while four in a row land 2 past a multiple of 4, so the count itself decides the pattern.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of sums of consecutive numbers, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving sums of consecutive numbers, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what happens to a total when plus and minus signs are placed between numbers, and determine that any signed arrangement stays even or odd in exactly the same way as the plain sum of the same numbers. They will explain that flipping one sign changes the value by twice that number, and twice any number is even, so the parity can never shift however the signs fall.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the remainders of two even numbers on division by 4 reveal about their sum, and determine that the sum is a multiple of 4 when both leave remainder 0 or both leave remainder 2, and misses only in the mixed case. They will explain that two spare 2s join into a full group of 4, while a lone spare 2 leaves the sum short, so the remainders alone decide the outcome.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what a shared divisor of two numbers means for their sum and their difference, and determine that any number dividing both M and N also divides M plus N and M minus N. They will explain that M and N are each a whole count of equal groups, so joining them or taking one from the other still leaves whole groups, which settles every case rather than a tested few.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what being divisible by a number means for that number's own factors and its multiples, and determine that divisibility passes down to every factor but not up to larger multiples. They will explain that each group of k splits evenly into smaller factor groups so a factor fits exactly, while every multiple keeps the original divisors because multiplying only repeats the same groups again.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of how divisibility passes to factors and multiples, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Seeing a Pattern, Then Proving It
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving how divisibility passes to factors and multiples, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the closing digits of a number decide about divisibility by 2, 4, and 8, and determine that the units digit settles 2, the last two digits settle 4, and the last three digits settle 8. They will explain that place value is the reason, since 10 is a multiple of 2, 100 a multiple of 4, and 1000 a multiple of 8, so every higher place drops out cleanly.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of last-digit tests for 2, 4, and 8, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving last-digit tests for 2, 4, and 8, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the sum of a number's digits reveals about divisibility by 9 and by 3, and determine that a number is divisible by 9 or by 3 exactly when its digit sum is. They will explain that each place value sits one above a multiple of 9 and of 3, so every digit leaves only itself behind, and that a number can pass the 3 test yet fail the 9 test.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of the digit-sum test for 9 and 3, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the digit-sum test for 9 and 3, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what an alternating add and subtract of the digits reveals about divisibility by 11, and determine that a number is divisible by 11 when this alternating total is 0 or a multiple of 11. They will explain that place values sit one above or one below a multiple of 11 in turn, so the plus and minus signs track those gaps and only their alternating sum is left over.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what folding a number's digits down to a single digit produces, and determine that this digital root equals the remainder the number leaves on division by 9. They will explain that each folding step keeps the mod 9 remainder unchanged, so the final single digit carries it, with the one wording exception that a multiple of 9 shows a digital root of 9 while its true remainder is 0.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that two numbers with no common factor other than 1 are called co-prime, and that two divisibility tests may be combined only when the two divisors are co-prime. They will decide whether a given pair is co-prime and say which pairs of tests may be combined to test a given divisor.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what testing two separate factors decides about divisibility by their product, and determine that passing both forces divisibility only when the two factors share no common factor. They will explain that 6 splits into 2 and 3 and 24 into 3 and 8, while 4 and 6 fail for 24 because their shared factor of 2 is counted once, so their combined guarantee reaches only 12.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of combining coprime factors, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Divisibility Shortcuts and Why They Work
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving combining coprime factors, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Digits in Disguise
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the units column of a letter addition puzzle fixes first, and determine that starting there pins the last digit of the answer and the carry into the next column, which then drives the column to its left. They will explain that two different letters never share a digit and no leading letter is 0, so each letter is reasoned out column by column along the carries rather than guessed.

objectives.strand_name: Digits in Disguise
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of solving addition cryptarithms, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Digits in Disguise
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving solving addition cryptarithms, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Digits in Disguise
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the units digit of a letter multiplication puzzle narrows down, and determine that the units digits multiplied must end in the puzzle's units letter, while the number of digits in the product limits how large the leading letter can be. They will explain that a leader too large would overflow into an extra digit, and repeated result letters give further checks, so the answer is reasoned out step by step.

summary_stats.counts_note: One distinct tool per concept; each tool runs four mods (AI demo, Learn, Practice, Free Play), with one objective each for AI demo, Learn and Practice and none for Free Play.
summary_stats.videos_note: One 30 to 40 second curiosity hook video per topic, plus a chapter intro video and a chapter summary video of 1 to 2 minutes each.
summary_stats.tool_needed_note: Per-item boolean for how the ANSWER is entered, NOT whether to show the tool. The frontend ALWAYS renders the tool. true = the answer must be produced through the tool. false = the student reasons it out (typed/spoken) and the tool stays on screen as an aid.
summary_stats.solved_examples_note: Each solved example carries a first-person 'reasoning' field that generalises the method.
summary_stats.practice_problems_note: 177 practice items in all = (12 microconcepts x 10 tool-answered) + (12 x 4 reasoning items) + 9 proof items on the concepts that state a general claim.
summary_stats.question_repository_note: Worked-example and practice questions are no longer inline. Each learn/practice concept carries a question_bank_ref into question_repository.json; the teacher agent pulls questions from the repository at teach time. The teaching (AI-demo) concept keeps its inline source_ai_reasoning block.

authoring_rules.nesting: Each objective contains exactly one concept; each concept contains its solved examples then its practice questions.
authoring_rules.solved_examples: At least 10 per microconcept; each is demonstrated on that section's tool with numbered steps, a final answer and first-person reasoning that models how to think, not just which buttons to press.
authoring_rules.practice_questions: At least 10 tool-answered items per microconcept (marked right/wrong on the tool), followed by exactly 4 reasoning items: application, reverse, explain, error_spotting. A concept that states a general claim carries a 5th reasoning item, proof, between explain and error_spotting.

The student answers the tool-answered practice questions that reinforce the worked examples.
